cards.headline: You can own a piece of a company.
cards.body: A stock is a unit of ownership in a real business. Buy one share of a company and you own a tiny slice of everything it owns and everything it earns. Not a lottery ticket. A claim.

art.alt: An investor holds one glowing ownership tile from a neighborhood bakery divided into real business slices.

cards.headline: Ownership is measured in shares.
cards.body: A company divides itself into shares. If it has issued 1,000 shares and you hold 10, you own **one percent** of the business — today, tomorrow, and every day until you sell.

art.alt: Equal paper ownership pieces move from a company into the matching slots of a physical shareholder ledger.

cards.title: Who owns a company

art.alt: Three paper ownership groups hold interlocking sections that assemble into one complete company ownership wheel.

cards.caption: In this example, founders hold **45%**, funds hold **34%**, and the public holds **21%**. Together, every shareholder owns exactly 100% of the company.

cards.body: A share is not just a number on a screen. It carries three real rights that come with being an owner.

cards.prompt: A company's share price doubles overnight. What happens to the percentage of the company you own?
cards.explanation: Price changes what your slice is **worth**, not how big it is. Your ownership percentage only moves if the company issues new shares or buys some back.

cards.headline: Owners are not lenders.
cards.body: Lend a company money and you are a bondholder: you get fixed interest, then your money back. Own a share and you get whatever is left after everyone else is paid. More risk. More upside.

art.alt: A paper-craft owner holds a piece of the business beside branching upside and downside paths, while a lender holds a fixed note and a straight repayment path.

cards.body: Shareholders get paid last — after employees, suppliers, and [[1]] have all been paid.
cards.explanation: That last-in-line position is exactly why shares carry more risk than bonds — and why they can be worth so much more when a business does well.

cards.headline: So why buy a slice at all?
cards.body: Two reasons, and only two. The business grows, so each slice becomes worth more. Or the business hands cash back to owners as a dividend. Everything else in investing is detail stacked on top.

art.name: owner-outcomes
art.alt: Three owner outcomes: business growth, cash dividends, or loss.

cards.summary: A share is legal ownership of a real business, not a ticket on a moving number.
bullets: Shares divide a company into equal, tradable slices.
Your ownership percentage does not change when the price does.
Owners are paid after lenders — more risk, and more upside.

art.alt: An investor holds one glowing ownership tile from a neighborhood bakery divided into real business slices.

cards.insight: You are not buying a price. You are buying a fraction of a business, and the price is only today's opinion of what that fraction is worth.
